patient.name: Patricia Mensah
patient.complaint: Hot, swollen right knee and fever for 2 days; cannot walk on it
background: Takes methotrexate weekly and prednisolone 5 mg daily
Right knee steroid injection 3 weeks ago
Lives alone in Lewisham; no drug allergies

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a single hot, swollen joint and fever, or 'Which is the most likely causative organism?' where age, IV drug use or sexual history picks the bug.

points: Patricia, 68, has **rheumatoid arthritis** on methotrexate and prednisolone.
Two days of a **hot, swollen right knee**.
She cannot bear weight; she feels shivery and sweaty.
Knee injected with steroid 3 weeks ago.

steps.lead: A single hot knee plus fever: think **septic arthritis** first. In an older patient the likeliest organism is **Staph aureus**.
Patricia has three risk factors: **RA**, immunosuppression with **methotrexate and steroids**, and a recent joint **injection**.

points: Any passive movement is agonising; range of movement markedly reduced.
Other joints at her usual RA baseline.
She is sweaty, with low-normal blood pressure.

steps.lead: Hot, swollen, immobile, tender joint, unable to weight-bear, plus **systemic signs** (fever, sweating, BP 98/60): the classic picture.

steps.q: Patricia's RA usually flares in her hands. What is the safest working diagnosis for this knee?
steps.r: A single hot joint with fever in an immunosuppressed patient is **septic arthritis until proven otherwise**. Never call it an RA flare without aspirating.

steps.text: Do not blame a hot joint on the patient's known arthritis. RA patients on **methotrexate or steroids** are exactly the ones who get septic joints, and steroids can blunt the fever.

steps.lead: The organism follows the patient: **IV drug use** points to Pseudomonas, a recent sore throat or skin infection to Strep, a young sexually active patient to **gonococcus**.
Patricia is an adult, but if a **child** came in limping, Kocher's criteria would sort septic arthritis from transient synovitis.

visual.title: Kocher's criteria (child with a limp)
visual.label: Example child: 3 points
visual.caption: One point each: non-weight bearing, fever >38.5°C, WCC >12×10⁹/L, ESR >40 mm/hr. Three points means a 93% probability.

steps.text: Count the four criteria; each point sharply raises the probability.

steps.lead: Kocher's criteria are the named rule to know for **children**: score 0 to 4, higher is more likely septic.

steps.text: A child with a new limp, fever above 38.5°C and refusal to bear weight is **septic arthritis** until aspirated. Transient synovitis is the diagnosis of exclusion.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (joint aspiration before antibiotics) or a synovial fluid result to interpret against crystals.

steps.q: Patricia is febrile and the registrar wants to start IV antibiotics now. What should happen first?
o: Joint aspiration for Gram stain and culture
steps.r: **Aspirate first**, then give antibiotics, so the culture identifies the organism. Antibiotics first can sterilise the fluid.

steps.lead: Patricia's knee is aspirated under **sterile** conditions before her first antibiotic dose. Culture of that fluid is the **gold standard**.

steps.title: Synovial fluid and bloods
steps.text: Purulent fluid, neutrophils above 90%, no crystals and cocci in clusters: **Staph aureus** septic arthritis.

visual.title: Synovial fluid white cell count
visual.label: Patricia 85,000
visual.caption: Septic fluid usually has a WCC above 10,000/mm³ (can reach 100,000) with neutrophils above 90%.

steps.lead: Patricia's fluid is purulent with **94% neutrophils**. A negative Gram stain would **not** have excluded infection: it is negative in 30 to 50%.

steps.title: Reading the aspirate
head: Fluid
Crystals
Most likely
rows: Turbid, neutrophils >90%, Gram stain or culture positive

steps.text: Crystals do not rule out infection: gout and sepsis can coexist. And a **negative Gram stain** never excludes septic arthritis; wait for culture and treat on clinical grounds.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' with the answer IV flucloxacillin after aspiration, vancomycin if penicillin allergic or MRSA risk, and washout when it fails to settle.

steps.lead: Patricia's knee cartilage is being destroyed by the hour. Treat it as an **emergency**: analgesia, rest the joint, act fast.

steps.title: Suspected septic joint: the order matters
nodes: Send for urgent Gram stain and culture
Washout or drainage of the joint
steps.caption: Aspiration comes before the first antibiotic dose; do not let it delay antibiotics for long.

steps.lead: Patricia has **no penicillin allergy** and no MRSA history, so after aspiration she starts **IV flucloxacillin**.

steps.q: If Patricia had a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin, which IV antibiotic would replace flucloxacillin?
steps.r: **Vancomycin** covers Staph aureus including MRSA and is not a beta-lactam. The other three are all penicillins.

steps.lead: Antibiotics alone are not enough: the pus must come out. Patricia goes for **joint washout/drainage**.

visual.title: Patricia's response to treatment
visual.caption: CRP falling and fever settling means it is working. If fevers continue and CRP does not fall, go back for washout.

steps.text: Her fever settled by day 4. Track inflammatory markers to decide if treatment is working.

steps.lead: Had Patricia's fever and CRP not settled, or the effusion kept coming back after aspiration, she would need **(repeat) surgical washout**.

steps.text: Course length is a favourite: IV antibiotics for **at least 2 weeks**, then oral for a further **4 to 6 weeks**.
Do not inject steroid into a hot joint until infection is excluded. Patricia's recent injection may be how the bacteria got in.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the route of infection, why cartilage is destroyed so fast, or why a prosthetic joint infection is so hard to clear (biofilm).

steps.lead: Patricia's bacteria probably arrived by **direct inoculation** from her steroid injection; blood-borne spread is the other common route.

steps.title: How a septic joint destroys cartilage
nodes: Bacterial toxins and host proteases released
steps.caption: The host's own enzymes do much of the damage, which is why speed matters.

steps.lead: This is why Patricia's knee is an emergency: **proteolytic enzymes** and toxins chew through cartilage fast.
If Patricia had a **knee replacement**, bacteria could hide in a **biofilm** on the metal, out of reach of antibiotics and neutrophils.

steps.q: Why does a prosthetic joint infection often need surgery rather than antibiotics alone?
o: Biofilm on the implant shields the bacteria
steps.r: A **biofilm** on the implant surface protects bacteria from antibiotics and immune cells, so washout or revision is often needed.

steps.lead: Kocher's criteria combine **systemic inflammation** (fever, ESR, WCC) with **function** (non-weight bearing) to estimate pre-test probability in children.
Gonococcal arthritis starts as a **disseminated** infection: flitting joint pains, tenosynovitis and skin pustules, then settles in one joint.

visual.title: Synovial neutrophil percentage
visual.label: Patricia 94%
visual.caption: A neutrophil-dominated fluid is the intense response that releases cartilage-destroying enzymes.

mcq.q: Which joint is most commonly affected by septic arthritis?
Which organism most commonly causes septic arthritis in elderly patients?
Which organism is the commonest cause in young, sexually active patients?
Which is NOT one of Kocher's criteria?
mcq.r: The four are non-weight bearing, fever >38.5°C, WCC >12×10⁹/L and ESR >40. CRP is not one.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard investigation for septic arthritis?
mcq.r: **Synovial fluid culture** from aspiration confirms it.

mcq.q: In roughly what proportion of septic arthritis is the Gram stain negative?
mcq.r: Negative in **30 to 50%**, so it cannot exclude infection.

mcq.q: What is the first-line empirical antibiotic?
mcq.r: **IV flucloxacillin**; vancomycin if penicillin allergic or MRSA risk.

mcq.q: How long is the usual antibiotic course?
o: At least 2 weeks IV, then 4–6 weeks oral
mcq.r: At least **2 weeks IV**, then **4 to 6 weeks oral**.

mcq.q: Why are prosthetic joints especially vulnerable to persistent infection?
o: Bacteria form biofilms on the implant
Implants are always colonised at surgery
mcq.r: **Biofilm** protects bacteria from antibiotics and immune defences.

mcq.q: What mainly destroys the cartilage in septic arthritis?
o: Bacterial toxins and host proteolytic enzymes
mcq.r: Neutrophil and bacterial **enzymes** degrade cartilage rapidly.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man has a 2 day history of a painful, swollen left knee. He has rheumatoid arthritis and takes methotrexate. He cannot bear weight. His temperature is 38.7°C. The knee is hot and red with a large effusion, and passive movement is very painful. Synovial fluid is turbid. No crystals are seen.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis of a single hot joint: infection versus crystals versus flare.
Immunosuppressed RA patient, fever, hot immobile joint, turbid fluid, no crystals.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fever plus one hot joint in an immunosuppressed patient: **septic arthritis**.

elim: No crystals were seen; gout needs negatively birefringent needles.
OA does not cause fever or turbid fluid.
No crystals; pseudogout needs positively birefringent rhomboids.
An RA flare is usually polyarticular; fever plus a single turbid joint is infection.

steps.x: **E. Septic arthritis.** Rule: monoarthritis + fever + no crystals = septic until proven otherwise.

technique.stem: A 45 year old woman has a 1 day history of a hot, swollen right knee. She is unable to bear weight. Her temperature is 38.4°C and pulse rate 104 bpm. She has not yet received any antibiotics.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Joint aspiration for Gram stain and culture
Plain X-ray of the right knee

steps.x: It asks for the initial investigation, so pick the test that both diagnoses and must come before antibiotics.
Acute hot joint with fever; the stem stresses no antibiotics yet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Aspirate the joint** before antibiotics so culture can grow the organism.

elim: Useful, but they do not sample the joint and are not the key first test.
Supports infection but cannot confirm it or identify the organism.
Slow and not needed to diagnose a septic joint.
Normal early; it shows damage only late.

steps.x: **C. Joint aspiration for Gram stain and culture.** Rule: aspirate first, then antibiotics.

technique.stem: A 64 year old woman has septic arthritis of the right knee. Synovial fluid has been sent for Gram stain and culture. She has no drug allergies and no history of MRSA. Her temperature is 38.6°C and BP 112/70 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management after aspiration: choose the empirical antibiotic and route.
Fluid already sent, so start antibiotics now; no allergy, no MRSA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Empirical **IV flucloxacillin** to cover Staph aureus.

elim: Steroid into an infected joint worsens infection.
Reserved for penicillin allergy or MRSA risk; she has neither.
Oral and wrong spectrum; septic arthritis needs IV anti-staphylococcal cover.
Oral is for step-down after at least 2 weeks IV.

steps.x: **B. IV flucloxacillin.** Vancomycin only if penicillin allergic or MRSA risk.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man has septic arthritis of the left knee. Aspiration is delayed for 5 days. An X-ray at 3 weeks shows loss of joint space. His temperature on arrival was 38.8°C.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his joint damage?
o: Bacterial toxins and host proteolytic enzymes degrading cartilage
Formation of osteophytes from abnormal loading
Pannus invading bone at the joint margins
Reduced blood supply causing avascular necrosis

steps.x: A mechanism question: why did the cartilage go so fast?
Known septic joint, treatment delayed, rapid cartilage loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Neutrophil influx releases **proteolytic enzymes**; bacteria release toxins; cartilage is digested.

elim: That is gout; no crystals here.
That is osteoarthritis, a slow process.
That is rheumatoid arthritis.
AVN affects bone, not cartilage, and is not caused by infection here.

steps.x: **A. Bacterial toxins and host proteolytic enzymes degrading cartilage.** That is why septic arthritis is an emergency.

practice.stem:
A 69 year old woman has a 2 day history of a painful, swollen right knee and rigors. She has rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and prednisolone. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 114 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg. The knee is hot with a tense effusion and she cannot bear weight.

Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, hypotension and a single hot joint with neutrophilic fluid and no crystals is septic arthritis. An RA flare would not give organisms on Gram stain.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a single hot joint with systemic upset.
Immunosuppressed, febrile, hypotensive, monoarthritis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fever, sepsis and turbid neutrophilic fluid with cocci: **septic arthritis**.

elim: No crystals; gout gives negatively birefringent needles.
No crystals; pseudogout gives positively birefringent rhomboids.
Follows a gut or genital infection; fluid is sterile and it is rarely this septic.
RA flares are polyarticular and do not give rigors with Gram-positive cocci.

steps.x: **E. Septic arthritis.** Don't call it an RA flare in a febrile immunosuppressed patient.

practice.stem: A 78 year old man has a 3 day history of a hot, swollen left knee. He has type 2 diabetes. His temperature is 38.5°C and pulse rate 102 bpm. Synovial fluid is purulent. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Gram-positive cocci in clusters in an elderly patient is Staphylococcus aureus, the commonest cause. Streptococci form chains.

steps.x: Organism question: use age and Gram stain.
Elderly patient; cocci in clusters.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clusters in an older adult: **Staph aureus**.

elim: A Gram-negative rod; an uncommon cause.
Gram-negative diplococci in young, sexually active adults.
Gram-negative rod linked to IV drug use.
Gram-positive cocci in chains, after throat or skin infection.

steps.x: **D. Staphylococcus aureus.** The commonest cause overall, especially in the elderly.

practice.stem: A 22 year old man has a 2 day history of a hot, swollen right knee. A week earlier he had dysuria and a urethral discharge. He has had flitting pains in his wrists and a few pustules on his hands. His temperature is 38.2°C. Synovial fluid Gram stain shows Gram-negative diplococci.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Urethritis, migratory polyarthralgia, skin lesions and Gram-negative diplococci are disseminated gonococcal infection. Chlamydia causes a sterile reactive arthritis.

steps.x: Organism question in a young man.
Young, urethritis, migratory arthralgia, skin pustules, Gram-negative diplococci.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Disseminated gonococcal infection: **Neisseria gonorrhoeae**.

elim: Causes reactive arthritis with sterile fluid; not seen as diplococci.
Gram-negative rods, in IV drug users.
Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
Gram-positive cocci in chains.

steps.x: **B. Neisseria gonorrhoeae.** Commonest cause in young, sexually active patients.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man who injects heroin has a 3 day history of a painful, swollen right knee. He is confused and sweating. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 94/60 mmHg. Synovial fluid is turbid and the Gram stain shows Gram-negative bacilli.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: In an IV drug user, Gram-negative bacilli point to Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Staph aureus would be Gram-positive cocci.

steps.x: Organism question: risk factor plus Gram stain.
IV drug use, confusion, sweating, Gram-negative rods.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IVDU with Gram-negative bacilli: **Pseudomonas aeruginosa**.

elim: Gram-negative too, but not the classic IVDU organism.
Gram-negative diplococci, not bacilli.
Gram-positive cocci, not Gram-negative bacilli.
Gram-positive cocci in chains.

steps.x: **C. Pseudomonas aeruginosa.** Pseudomonas in IV drug users, often with confusion and sweating.

practice.stem:
A 6 year old boy has a 2 day history of a limp and now refuses to walk on his right leg. His temperature is 39.0°C and pulse rate 128 bpm. The right hip is held flexed and any movement is painful.

Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: This child meets all four Kocher criteria (non-weight bearing, fever >38.5°C, WCC >12, ESR >40), giving a 99% probability of septic arthritis. Transient synovitis scores 0 to 1.

steps.x: A limping child: use Kocher's criteria.
Non-weight bearing, fever >38.5°C, WCC >12, ESR >40: all four.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Kocher 4/4 means a 99% probability: **septic arthritis**.

elim: Chronic arthritis over at least 6 weeks; not an acute febrile hip.
Painless or mild limp over weeks, afebrile, normal markers.
Overweight adolescents, afebrile.
Usually afebrile, weight bearing, normal markers: Kocher 0 to 1.

steps.x: **C. Septic arthritis.** Kocher 4/4 = 99%; transient synovitis scores low.

practice.stem: A 41 year old woman has a 4 day history of a hot, swollen left knee. Ten days ago she had a sore throat with fever that settled without treatment. Her temperature is 38.3°C and pulse rate 106 bpm. Synovial fluid is turbid and the Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in chains.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Gram-positive cocci in chains after a recent pharyngitis point to Streptococcus. Staph aureus forms clusters.

steps.x: Organism question: preceding infection plus Gram stain.
Recent pharyngitis; cocci in chains.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Streptococcus species after pharyngitis: **Streptococcus pyogenes**.

elim: Gram-negative diplococci.
Gram-negative bacilli, in IV drug users.
Cocci in clusters, not chains.
Coagulase-negative clusters, mainly prosthetic joints.

steps.x: **E. Streptococcus pyogenes.** Chains = strep; clusters = staph.

practice.stem: A 59 year old man has a 1 day history of a hot, swollen right knee. He is unable to bear weight. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. The doctor plans to start IV antibiotics.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Joint aspiration with Gram stain and culture
practice.e: Joint aspiration for Gram stain and culture is gold standard and must precede antibiotics. Serum urate can be normal in acute gout and never excludes sepsis.

steps.x: Initial investigation before antibiotics.
Hot joint, fever, antibiotics about to start.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Aspirate the joint **first**, then give antibiotics.

elim: Helpful but do not replace sampling the joint.
Not needed for diagnosis.
Delays treatment and does not identify the organism.
Normal or high in gout and does not exclude infection.

steps.x: **C. Joint aspiration with Gram stain and culture.** Gold standard, and done before antibiotics.

practice.stem:
A 66 year old woman has a 2 day history of a hot, swollen left knee. Her temperature is 38.4°C. Synovial fluid is turbid and yellow with no crystals. The Gram stain is negative.

Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of these results?
o: Infection is excluded by the negative Gram stain
Repeat aspiration is needed before any treatment
Septic arthritis remains likely; await culture
practice.e: Purulent fluid with neutrophils above 90% and a high WCC is septic arthritis until culture says otherwise; the Gram stain is negative in 30 to 50% of cases.

steps.x: An interpretation question: does a negative Gram stain exclude infection?
Fever; purulent fluid with very high neutrophils; no crystals; Gram stain negative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Purulent fluid means **septic arthritis** is still likely; culture will decide.

elim: Gout needs needle-shaped crystals; none were seen.
Gram stain is negative in 30 to 50% of septic joints.
OA fluid is clear with a low WCC.
Treat now on clinical grounds; do not delay for repeat tests.

steps.x: **E. Septic arthritis remains likely; await culture.** Gram stain misses 30 to 50%.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman has septic arthritis of the right knee. The joint has been aspirated and fluid sent for culture. She had anaphylaxis to amoxicillin 10 years ago. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Penicillin anaphylaxis rules out flucloxacillin, benzylpenicillin and co-amoxiclav; IV vancomycin covers Staph aureus including MRSA.

steps.x: Initial management with a penicillin allergy.
Aspiration done; true penicillin anaphylaxis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Swap flucloxacillin for **IV vancomycin**.

elim: A penicillin: contraindicated after anaphylaxis.
Contains amoxicillin: contraindicated.
First line normally, but it is a penicillin.
Oral and inadequate for a septic joint.

steps.x: **D. IV vancomycin.** Vancomycin if penicillin allergic or MRSA risk.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man has septic arthritis of the left knee caused by Staphylococcus aureus. He had a joint washout and has now completed 2 weeks of IV flucloxacillin. His fever has settled and his CRP has fallen from 240 to 12 mg/L.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Continue IV flucloxacillin for a further 6 months
Switch to oral antibiotics for a further 4–6 weeks
practice.e: After at least 2 weeks of IV antibiotics with clinical and biochemical response, step down to oral antibiotics for a further 4 to 6 weeks.

steps.x: Next step after an IV course.
Responding well after 2 weeks IV.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Step down to **oral antibiotics for 4 to 6 weeks**.

elim: Far too long; switch to oral once improving.
Steroid into a recently infected joint is wrong.
Not needed: he has responded.
Too short: he needs another 4 to 6 weeks orally.

steps.x: **E. Switch to oral antibiotics for a further 4–6 weeks.** At least 2 weeks IV, then 4 to 6 weeks oral.

practice.stem:
A 74 year old woman with a right total knee replacement has septic arthritis of that knee. She has had IV vancomycin for 6 days and three aspirations, but the effusion keeps returning. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.

Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Add oral rifampicin and review in 2 weeks
practice.e: Persistent effusion despite serial aspirations, continuing fever and a static CRP, especially with a prosthesis, are indications for surgical washout.

steps.x: Next step when treatment is failing.
Prosthetic joint; persistent effusion despite serial aspirations; ongoing fever; CRP not falling.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Orthopaedic **surgical washout**.

elim: Waiting does not deal with the persistent collection.
Contraindicated in infection.
Serial aspirations have already failed.
Step-down is only after response; she is not improving.

steps.x: **D. Surgical washout of the joint.** Washout if not improving, especially with a prosthesis.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man had a left total hip replacement 8 months ago. He now has a third episode of septic arthritis of that hip with the same Staphylococcus organism, despite completing full antibiotic courses each time. His temperature is 37.9°C and pulse rate 96 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for the persistent infection?
o: Antibiotics cannot cross into synovial fluid
Bacterial biofilm on the implant surface
Hypersensitivity reaction to the metal implant
Urate crystal deposition around the implant
practice.e: Bacteria form biofilms on prosthetic surfaces, evading antibiotics and host defences, so infection recurs despite full courses.

steps.x: Mechanism question about a prosthetic joint.
Implant, same organism recurring, antibiotics keep failing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bacteria in a **biofilm** on the implant evade antibiotics and immune cells.

elim: Antibiotics do reach synovial fluid; that is how most septic joints are cured.
Possible in theory, but recurrent infection only at the implant points to biofilm.
That is aseptic loosening, not recurrent infection.
That is gout, not infection.

steps.x: **B. Bacterial biofilm on the implant surface.** Why prosthetic joints often need surgery.

IV at least 2 weeks, then oral 4–6 weeks

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: failing to settle or prosthetic = washout.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: three routes, then enzymes.

glossary.Septic arthritis: Bacterial infection inside a joint space; a medical emergency because cartilage is destroyed quickly.
glossary.Staphylococcus aureus: Gram-positive coccus in clusters; the commonest cause of septic arthritis.
glossary.MSSA: Meticillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, treatable with flucloxacillin.
glossary.MRSA: Meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus; needs vancomycin rather than flucloxacillin.
glossary.Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Gram-negative bacillus; linked to septic arthritis in IV drug users.
glossary.Neisseria gonorrhoeae: Gram-negative diplococcus causing gonorrhoea; commonest septic arthritis cause in young sexually active adults.
glossary.Gonococcal arthritis: Joint infection from disseminated gonorrhoea, often after migratory joint pains and skin lesions.
glossary.Gram-negative diplococci: Paired bean-shaped bacteria that stain pink; classic for Neisseria.
glossary.Gram stain: Rapid microscopy stain separating bacteria into Gram-positive (purple) and Gram-negative (pink).
glossary.Kocher's criteria: Four-point score (non-weight bearing, fever, WCC, ESR) estimating septic arthritis risk in a limping child.
glossary.Transient synovitis: Self-limiting, non-infective hip inflammation in children, often after a viral illness.
glossary.Arthrocentesis: Needle aspiration of fluid from a joint.
glossary.Joint aspiration: Drawing synovial fluid out of a joint with a needle for testing.
glossary.Synovial fluid: The lubricating fluid inside a joint; sampled to look for infection or crystals.
glossary.Washout: Surgical flushing of an infected joint to remove pus and bacteria.
glossary.Flucloxacillin: Penicillinase-resistant penicillin active against Staph aureus; first-line for septic arthritis.
glossary.Vancomycin: Glycopeptide antibiotic used for MRSA or penicillin allergy.
glossary.Biofilm: A slimy layer of bacteria stuck to a surface that shields them from antibiotics and immune cells.
glossary.Direct inoculation: Bacteria introduced straight into the joint by trauma, surgery or injection.
glossary.Osteomyelitis: Infection of bone, which can spread into an adjacent joint.
glossary.ESR: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate; a non-specific marker of inflammation.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein; an inflammatory marker that rises in infection and falls with treatment.
glossary.Methotrexate: Disease-modifying drug for RA that suppresses the immune system.
glossary.Urethritis: Inflammation of the urethra, causing dysuria and discharge.
glossary.Epididymitis: Inflammation of the epididymis, behind the testis.
glossary.Pharyngitis: Sore throat from inflammation of the pharynx.
glossary.Negatively birefringent: Crystal optics on polarised light typical of urate crystals in gout.
